newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FORECAST - Swedish repo rate seen at floor-survey.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Swedish repo rate seen at floor-survey.

text.p: The Swedish repurchase rate will bottom out at its current level of 4.10 percent, six of 10 economists in a Reuter poll forecast.
But they do not expect any increase of the rate until 1998 and no one expected the Swedish central bank, the Riksbank, to lower the rate on Tuesday.
"The main scenario is for the repo to remain steady in all of 1997 and to be raised in 1998," Anders Hahnel, economist at Aragon, told Reuters.
"We could see a cut if the private consumption would develop much weaker (than expected) but I think the Riksbank wants to wait for the effects of previous cuts. In addition the crown is too weak."
Economists who believe in further cuts say the crown needs to strengthen to trade below 120 at the trade weighted (TCW) index compared to its current level of about 124.
The crown has softened from 4.41 against the mark on December 17 and from 4.34 in October. It was trading at 4.57 at midday today.
The Riksbank lowered the repo rate 25 times to 4.10 percent from 8.91 percent at the beginning of last year, but has not moved the rate this year.
The Riksbank's lending and deposit rates are currently at 5.25 percent and 3.75 percent, respectively.
Four of 10 analysts surveyed said they believed in further cuts.

"The Riksbank can cut the rate further since inflation continues to be low, the crown is undervalued and will strengthen while wage increases will be within reasonable levels," said Bjorn Englund, economist at Unibank.
"I believe the floor is at 3.75 percent and that we will see a cut to 3.80 percent before the summer," he said, adding that crown strengthening would be necessary.
"The TCW must fall below 120 and the crown must strengthen to between 4.40 and 4.43 against the mark," Englund said.
Sources who participated in this survey are: Aragon, Carnegie, Hagstromer & Qviberg, Handelsbanken, HSBC Midland, Nordbanken, S-E-Banken, Swedbank, Unibank and Ohman.
